_comment_les: 'max. initial strain rate S_ijS_ij' is max(S_ij S_ij) over the *initial* field,
recorded once by initialise_flow_fields and never overwritten. It is written by
every LES case but only gated where a reference.json lists it.
The pairing below is deliberate and gives the key two different meanings
depending on the reference value, because a metric only fails when every
applicable check fails. Where the reference is zero - LES_pipe_solidrotation,
whose initial field is u_theta = Omega*r, an exactly zero-strain state - the
relative check is skipped as ref is approximately 0 and the absolute 1e-20
stands alone as a hard machine-zero gate on the cylindrical velocity-gradient
assembly. A Cartesian assembly there differentiates the stored qy = r*u_r
instead of u_r and returns Omega^2/2 = 0.5, twenty orders above the bound.
Where the reference is a real nonzero strain, 1e-20 can never be met and the
relative check carries the test, as for any other flow quantity.
_comment_sgs_boundaries: The five keys below gate the subgrid coefficient where it is consumed - the
face sets the stress and enthalpy-flux terms actually multiply - not where it
is produced. They use the same dual-meaning abs/rel pairing documented above:
a metric fails only when every applicable check fails, so with a zero
reference the relative check is skipped and the 1e-20 absolute bound stands
alone as a hard machine-zero gate, while with a nonzero reference 1e-20 can
never be met and the relative check carries the test.
'max. sgs coefficient on physical walls' is the wall closure itself. For
wall-resolved LES at a no-slip wall the subgrid stress and enthalpy flux are
zero - WALE gives nu_sgs ~ y^3 as y->0 - so this is referenced at exactly 0
and gated at 1e-20. The molecular wall flux is unaffected and is not zero.
Note this is a wall-resolved statement; a wall model would not satisfy it.
'max. sgs coefficient at inlet/outlet' is the opposite gate. The inlet and
outlet are not walls, so subgrid transport must be *retained* there; the
zero-normal-gradient coefficient closure preserves the adjacent value. A
nonzero reference means a regression that zeroed the inflow coefficient along
with the wall one would fail the relative check. In a fully periodic case
there is no such plane and the reference is 0, where 1e-20 applies instead.
'min. sgs coefficient on stress/flux faces' is the positivity gate for the
cd2 coefficient interpolation. The compact C2P stencils undershoot a unit
peak by up to -0.36 (cp6) and can hand a negative eddy viscosity to the
stress terms; cd2 has both weights at +1/2 and cannot. Referenced at 0 - the
wall faces are exactly zero and no face may go below them. Non-negativity is
necessary, not sufficient: it does not on its own prove stability or
conservation and is not claimed to.
'min. total face viscosity (molecular+sgs)' checks the floor the momentum
stresses see. Isothermal flow must sit at exactly 1.0, the non-dimensional
molecular value, which is what proves the sgs part is added to a preserved
molecular interpolation rather than folded into one interpolation of the
total. Under variable properties the floor is the fluid's own min mu/mu0 and
is below 1, so this is relative-only: an absolute bound would encode one
fluid's property table.
'max. |sgs enthalpy flux|' gates the magnitude of subgrid heat transport, not
just its presence. It is relative-carried in a thermal case and pinned to
zero in an isothermal one.
_comment_mhd: The two MHD entries below are absolute-only on purpose. Both are round-off
residuals of the electric-potential projection, so their reproducible part is
their magnitude, not their digits: a relative check would fail across
decompositions for no physical reason. max|div(j)| sits near 1e-10 when the
projection is consistent and near 1e+2 when it is not, so 1e-8 separates the
two by ten orders of magnitude and still catches any real regression.
Both keys are now gated in the inlet-outlet case too. They were not before: its
all-Neumann electric-potential problem was incompatible at the outlet, where
(u x B).n is nonzero, so the solver projected that constant out and left a
uniform div(j) = (1/V) * closed_integral (u x B).n of 3.3e-3. Imposing the
insulating condition j.n = 0 on the cut planes removed it; the key is the
guard that stops it coming back.
Reading these keys for a case whose B has a nonzero z (or x) component at an
x cut plane: every case shipped today is wall-normal only, B = (0, By, 0). The
insulating condition is imposed pointwise, j_x = 0 at every face, which for a
wall-normal field is essentially exact - z-mirror symmetry gives <u_z> = 0, so
no mean axial current wants to cross. For an inclined field it is only an
approximation: a nonzero Bz can drive a real mean secondary flow <u_z>(y) /= 0
and recirculating current may legitimately cross the plane, where the only
guaranteed property is the integral one, closed_surface j_x dA = 0.
The trap is that these two metrics cannot tell the difference. div(j) = 0 is
enforced by construction once the face fluxes are dropped, so both stay at
round-off whatever B does - measured 2.9e-12 for B = (0,10,0) and 3.2e-10 for
B = (0,10,5) in MHD_channel_scp_inout_Tw. A green result here is therefore not
evidence that an inclined-field case is physically right; judge that on the
flow, not on these keys.

_comment: Per-case overrides, keyed by case directory name. An override replaces the
global entry for that metric outright, so omitting "abs" drops the absolute
check and leaves only the relative one.
'global mass balance' is fl%tt_mass_change, the volume integral of drho/dt.
In a periodic thermal case there is no boundary to carry mass in or out, so
as the fluid heats this integral is genuinely non-zero - 0.28 in
pipe_scp_periodic_Tw - and the global 1e-6 absolute tolerance can never be
met. Only its reproducibility is meaningful, so these cases keep the relative
check and drop the absolute one. Isothermal and inlet-outlet cases keep the
tight global tolerance, where a non-zero value really would be a defect.
'max. |div(current density)|' is an absolute residual, so its floor scales
with the size of j itself, and j scales with |B|. The two *_Btilt cases carry
B_static = (10, 20, 5), |B| = 22.9, and measure 2.0e-9 and 2.4e-9 against a
global tolerance of 1e-8 - passing, but with only four-fold headroom, which is
thin for a round-off quantity that moves with the decomposition. Dividing the
measured value by |B| recovers the same 1e-10 floor as the |B| = 1 parent
cases, so the global tolerance is scaled by |B| here rather than relaxed on a
